items.title: SGLang-Omni: The Model Was Never the Hard Part
items.summary: How SGLang serves a model that sees, hears, and talks back — and why it needed a whole new runtime on top of SGLang. The misconception I started with When I first heard about SGLang-Omni , I assumed I knew what it was. SGLang, the core project, is famous for making a single large language model fast — RadixAttention for KV-cache reuse, speculative decoding, a zero-overhead scheduler, all the clever tricks that squeeze more tokens per second out of a GPU. So “Omni,” I figured, must be the same bag of tricks applied to other modalities. Some radix-cache-like reuse for audio. Some speculative decoding for image tokens. Modality-specific algorithmic wins. That guess was wrong, and the way it was wrong turned out to be the interesting part. SGLang-Omni is not a set of per-modality algorithm optimizations. It’s a systems-level orchestration play . Its whole reason to exist is to take a model that isn’t one model at all — it’s a little committee of models that talk to each other — and decouple it into independent stages, so you can: put each stage on the right hardware, give each stage the scheduler it actually needs, scale up only the stage that’s the bottleneck, and contain a crash to one stage instead of taking down the whole request. In other words, the hard problem was never “make the model faster.” The model math was mostly already solved. The hard problem was serving it: how do you run a graph of cooperating models, streaming state between them in real time, across multiple GPUs, without the whole thing turning into a tangle? This post walks through how SGLang-Omni answers that, using Qwen3-Omni as the running example. We’ll follow one request from HTTP call to audio waveform, and along the way see why a plain script couldn’t do the job, how the pipeline is wired, and — importantly — how Omni leans on plain old SGLang for the heavy lifting rather than reinventing it. What Qwen3-Omni actually demands To see why Omni needed a new runtime, you have to look at what a modern omni-modal model actually is . Core SGLang is built to serve one autoregressive model behind one scheduler and one KV cache. Qwen3-Omni is a committee. Diagram 1 — The mental shift: one model vs a pipeline of stages. Qwen3-Omni isn’t a single autoregressive model. It’s built around two large decode backbones that hand off to each other: Thinker — the “understanding” brain. It takes text, images, video, and audio, fuses them, and generates text tokens. This is where the reasoning lives. Talker — the “speaking” brain. It takes Thinker’s output as it’s being produced and turns it into a stream of speech codec tokens, which a vocoder later turns into an actual waveform. Around those two, there’s a supporting cast: a vision encoder, an audio encoder, an aggregation step, a code predictor that fills in the fine detail of the audio codes, and a final vocoder. But the two things that dominate everything are Thinker and Talker. Here’s what makes this genuinely different from serving one LLM: Two backbones of roughly equal size. This is the crux. It’s not “one big model plus some small helpers.” Thinker and Talker are both heavy, both need continuous batching, both maintain a KV cache. The moment you have two comparably-sized models, you have a placement and resource-partitioning problem: do they share a GPU or not? If they share, how do you split GPU memory and KV cache between them — is 50/50 even right? If they don’t, how do you coordinate the traffic between devices? This is the real engineering pressure, far more than “supporting a vocoder.” Dual output. A single request can produce two results — a text answer and an audio answer. The system can’t just return whichever finishes first; it has to gather both. Real streaming between models. Talker doesn’t wait for Thinker to finish. It consumes Thinker’s hidden states token by token, so audio can start playing while the text is still being generated. A feedback loop. Talker and the Code Predictor play ping-pong: Talker emits one codec token, waits for the Code Predictor to send back an aggregated embedding, and only then takes its next step. None of these is a “just add a component” problem. They’re all about timing and coordination — who can run when, who’s waiting on whom, and where the intermediate state lives. That’s a scheduling and dataflow problem, and it’s exactly the kind of thing a single-model server isn’t built to express. Why a serial script — or even asyncio — can’t do it The natural first reaction is: if core SGLang doesn’t handle this, why not just write a function that chains the models together? # The most naive serial approach def process_request(request): state        = preprocess(request)                 # CPU image_embeds = image_encoder(state)                # GPU audio_embeds = audio_encoder(state)                # GPU — only starts after image_encoder finishes merged       = aggregate(state, image_embeds, audio_embeds)  # CPU text_tokens  = thinker(merged)                     # GPU:0 — next step only after thinker fully finishes text_result  = decode(text_tokens)                 # CPU codec_tokens = talker(text_tokens)                 # GPU:1 — only starts after thinker fully finishes codes        = code_predictor(codec_tokens)        # GPU:1 audio        = code2wav(codes)                     # GPU:1 return text_result, audio This runs . It’s also a performance disaster, and the reason is subtle enough to be worth a number. Talker has to wait until Thinker is completely done before it starts. Say Thinker generates 100 tokens at 30 ms each, and Talker takes 20 ms per step. Serial time-to-first-audio is roughly 3000 ms + 20 ms ≈ 3020 ms . But if Talker could consume Thinker’s tokens as they arrive , time-to-first-audio drops to about 30 ms + 20 ms ≈ 50 ms . That’s a ~60× difference in perceived latency, and it comes entirely from overlapping work that the serial version forces into a line. So the next instinct is: fine, use asyncio, fire the encoders off in parallel, stream Thinker into Talker. That’s better — it at least admits the stages can advance concurrently. But single-process async only pushes the real problems back one layer. Five of them survive: GPU-memory isolation. Thinker is on GPU:0, Talker on GPU:1. Managing multiple large models across multiple GPUs in one process couples their CUDA contexts, memory allocation, and error handling. One model’s OOM becomes everyone’s problem. Separate processes give each stage its own clean device view. Different scheduling policies. Thinker needs continuous batching, KV-cache management, and dynamic batch changes. The Code Predictor is a lightweight step-by-step forward. Cramming both into one scheduler means either a monstrous unified abstraction or a pile of special-cased local logic. Split into stages, each stage picks the executor and policy that fits it. Fault isolation. In production, one model hanging or crashing shouldn’t kill the whole request chain. Process boundaries turn a stage crash into a stage crash. Bottleneck-only scaling. If Thinker is the bottleneck, you want to scale just Thinker . If a request doesn’t need speech, you want to drop Talker / Code Predictor / vocoder entirely. Stages make that a config change, not a rewrite. Control/data separation. Multi-process doesn’t have to mean “copy tensors everywhere.” The trick — which we’ll get to — is to send tiny metadata between stages (“the data is at this shared-memory slot”) while the big tensors move over shared memory or CUDA IPC, near zero-copy. Put together, these push you toward a specific shape: a multi-process, asynchronous producer–consumer pipeline , where each stage is its own process, upstream stages produce incremental results, and downstream stages consume them at their own pace. That shape is SGLang-Omni. The answer: a pipeline of stages At the top, SGLang-Omni is three layers: Diagram 2 — The three-layer runtime. The Coordinator is the front door and the mailroom. It does exactly three things: wrap the incoming request and hand it to the first stage; wait for the terminal stages to report back and merge their results; and, if the user disconnects, broadcast an “abort” to everyone. Crucially, it does not route between stages — it doesn’t decide “where does the encoder’s output go next.” Each stage decides that for itself via its own get_next. The Coordinator is a gatekeeper and a gatherer, not a traffic cop. Stage → Worker → Executor is where a request actually gets computed. The Stage is a runtime shell: it receives messages, aggregates inputs when several upstream stages feed into it, and manages routing. The Worker is the execution unit inside a stage. The Executor is the thing that finally calls the model. Control plane + Data plane is how stages communicate — and this split is the single most important idea in the whole system. The waiter and the food runner Here’s the intuition. In a restaurant, the waiter carries the order ticket — small, fast, “table 4 wants the salmon.” The food runner carries the plate — big, heavy, needs care. You don’t make the waiter carry plates, and you don’t make the runner memorize orders. SGLang-Omni splits communication exactly this way: Control plane (ZMQ): the order tickets. Tens of bytes, microsecond latency. “Stage A finished; the result for request 7 is sitting in shared-memory slot 2.” That’s it. Data plane (the Relay): the plates. The actual tensors — encoder outputs, hidden states — move over shared memory, CUDA IPC, or NCCL, essentially zero-copy. They never touch ZMQ. Diagram 3 — Control plane vs data plane, and the credit system. The reason to separate them is that notifications and bulk data have opposite requirements. ZMQ is great for small control messages and terrible for moving giant tensors; shared memory and CUDA IPC are the reverse. Try to make one channel do both and you do neither well. The Relay also needs flow control , and it uses a beautifully simple mechanism: credits , which is really just a semaphore. Picture a fixed number of serving trays between two kitchen stations — say two trays. A “credit” is an empty tray. Upstream wants to send data → it takes a credit (grabs a tray), writes the tensor into that shared-memory slot, and sends a “data ready” ticket over ZMQ. Downstream reads the data → releases the credit (returns the tray) so upstream can reuse the slot. When all trays are full and downstream hasn’t caught up → upstream blocks . That’s backpressure , and it’s exactly what you want: a slow downstream naturally throttles a fast upstream instead of blowing up memory. This is why downstream stages are built to read incoming data as fast as they can — every read frees a tray and keeps the line moving. Add a model without touching the backbone One design choice makes this framework more than a Qwen3-Omni special case: the pipeline topology isn’t hardcoded. It’s declarative config . A model doesn’t inherit a fixed set of steps — it declares its own stage graph , and the framework compiles that into a runnable pipeline. # sglang_omni/models/qwen3_omni/config.py  (trimmed) class Qwen3OmniSpeechPipelineConfig(PipelineConfig): entry_stage     = "preprocessing" terminal_stages = ["decode", "code2wav"]        # two ends: text + speech gpu_placement   = {"thinker": 0, "talker_ar": 1, "code_predictor": 1, "code2wav": 1} stages = [ StageConfig("preprocessing", get_next=preprocessing_next, ...), StageConfig("image_encoder", get_next=encoder_next, ...), StageConfig("audio_encoder", get_next=encoder_next, ...), StageConfig("mm_aggregate",  get_next=aggregate_next, input_handler=AggregatedInput(sources=["preprocessing", "image_encoder", "audio_encoder"])), StageConfig("thinker", get_next=thinker_next_speech, stream_to=["talker_ar"]),               # stream hidden states StageConfig("decode", get_next=None),               # terminal StageConfig("talker_ar", get_next=talker_ar_next, stream_to=["code_predictor"]), StageConfig("code_predictor", get_next=code_predictor_next, stream_to=["code2wav", "talker_ar"]),   # dual path: output + feedback StageConfig("code2wav", get_next=None),             # terminal ] Notice how much of the system’s behavior is data here: which stage is the entry, which are terminals, which GPU each stage lives on, which stages stream to which. compile_pipeline() turns this into live processes. The payoff showed up when the team later added Ming-Omni , whose speech path uses a completely different approach (CFM/DiT flow-matching instead of Qwen3-Omni’s RVQ codec). The framework backbone barely changed — they wrote a new PipelineConfig and the model-specific executors, and the pipeline machinery just carried it. Model differences got pushed into config and executors, not into the runtime's core. There's even a variant mechanism so the same model can expose a 6-stage text-only pipeline and a 9-stage text-plus-speech pipeline, chosen at startup with --variant speech. Walk one request through the nine stages Let’s follow a “text + image + audio” request through Qwen3-Omni’s full speech pipeline. With speech output on, it’s nine stages : STAGE            ROLE               DEVICE   WHAT IT DOES ─────────────    ────────────────   ──────   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── preprocessing    Entry              CPU      Tokenize text; parse image/audio/video into tensors image_encoder    Encode             GPU      Vision Transformer → image embeddings audio_encoder    Encode             GPU      Mel-spectrogram encoder → audio embeddings aggregate        Fan-in             CPU      Merge text tokens with encoder outputs into one input thinker          Inference          GPU:0    MoE Transformer; generates text tokens (then fans out) decode           Output (terminal)  CPU      Turn token ids back into text talker_ar        Speech             GPU:1    Autoregressively generate speech codec tokens code_predictor   Speech             GPU:1    Fill in remaining RVQ code layers (feedback loop) code2wav         Speech (terminal)  GPU:1    Vocoder synthesizes the final audio waveform Diagram 4 — The Qwen3-Omni 9-stage pipeline. Note the fan-out (one input, many branches) at preprocessing and the fan-in (many branches, one input) at aggregate — plus the second fan-out at Thinker, where text and speech split. Reading the flow: Preprocessing (CPU) turns raw input into tensors and metadata. The instant it’s done, the result fans out to three places at once — the image encoder, the audio encoder, and the aggregate stage. True parallelism starts here, not at the model. Image & audio encoders (GPU) run independently and in parallel. The image encoder is a Vision Transformer; the audio encoder is a Transformer over Mel-spectrogram features. Each sends its embeddings to aggregate. Aggregate (CPU) is the classic fan-in node. It waits until all its upstream inputs have arrived, then merges the text tokens with the encoder outputs into a single input Thinker can consume in one shot. It does little compute — its job is synchronization . Thinker (GPU:0) is the semantic center. It embeds the tokens, injects the encoder outputs at the right placeholder positions, runs its Transformer stack, and generates text tokens. Then it fans out again — the most important branch in the system, because this is where text and speech formally split: A. the text branch sends the full result to decode; B. the speech branch streams to talker_ar token by token, passing along not just the token ids but Thinker's embeddings and a chosen layer's hidden states, so Talker can align to what Thinker meant. Decode (CPU, terminal) turns Thinker’s token ids back into text and reports completion. Talker AR → Code Predictor → Code2Wav (GPU:1) is the speech chain. Talker autoregressively generates codec tokens; the Code Predictor fills in the fine-grained RVQ layers (and feeds information back to Talker, more on that below); Code2Wav — a neural vocoder — accumulates codes and streams out 24 kHz audio chunks. When both terminals — decode and code2wav — report done, the Coordinator merges the text and the audio and returns them together. How Omni rides on SGLang Here’s the part I most misjudged at the start, and the part worth being precise about: SGLang-Omni is not a fork of SGLang. It’s an orchestration layer that sits on top of SGLang and treats it as a library for the compute-heavy work. Think of it as a division of labor: Diagram 5 — Omni owns the pipeline; SGLang owns the AR math The heavy autoregressive stages — Thinker and Talker — are the ones that need everything core SGLang is good at: continuous batching, KV-cache management, fast attention. So Omni doesn’t rebuild any of that. Those stages run through an EngineExecutor wrapping OmniEngine , a compact serving loop with its own Scheduler (picks requests, builds batches) and ModelRunner (runs the forward). And that ModelRunner stands on SGLang's shoulders — the Thinker model, for example, reuses: RadixAttention for efficient KV-cache management, SGLang’s fused kernels (like a fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel for a big speedup), and the same ModelRunner / forward / sampling machinery SGLang uses to serve a plain LLM. The lighter stages don’t need any of this. An image encoder is a one-shot operator: input in, forward once, output out. It runs through a much thinner DirectModelExecutor — no request state, no KV cache, no scheduler. This is the whole point of the Executor abstraction: class Executor(ABC): async def add_request(payload) -> None    # submit async def get_result() -> StagePayload     # collect async def abort(request_id) -> None        # cancel def set_stream_fn(fn) -> None              # streaming hook Same interface, wildly different implementations — a stateless forward for encoders, a stateful multi-step engine for Thinker and Talker. The pipeline doesn’t care which; it just calls add_request and awaits get_result. One more detail earns a single sentence: OmniEngine supports an overlap mode that runs the current step's GPU work while the CPU processes the previous step's results, the same GPU/CPU pipelining trick that made core SGLang's scheduler "zero-overhead." Omni reuses the idea rather than the exact code. So the mental model is: Omni owns when and where things run; SGLang owns how the autoregressive math runs. Everything speech-specific — encoders, vocoders, streaming audio, the pipeline itself — is Omni’s. The transformer decode loop is SGLang’s. The two clever tricks Most of the pipeline is boring in a good way: stage finishes, next stage picks up. But two relationships aren’t like that, and they’re where “temporal orchestration” stops being a phrase and starts being code. Diagram 6 — Streaming (Thinker→Talker) and the feedback loop (Talker↔Code Predictor). ① Streaming ( stream_to). Thinker doesn't hand Talker a finished paragraph. Every time it generates a token, it immediately pushes the corresponding hidden states out. Talker consumes them as a true producer–consumer stream: If Thinker is faster, a few tokens queue up and Talker catches up at its own pace. If Talker is faster, the queue empties and Talker simply awaits the next token. When Thinker finishes, it appends an end-of-text marker to the stream, and once Talker consumes it, Talker knows the text is done. There’s even a nice optimization on startup: if Talker finds several tokens already waiting when it begins, it prefills on the whole batch at once instead of crawling forward one token at a time. ② The feedback loop ( WAITING_FEEDBACK). This is the most intricate state transition in the system. Every time Talker emits a codec token, it can't just barrel ahead. It sends the token to the Code Predictor and deliberately parks itself in a WAITING_FEEDBACK state — and while it's parked, the scheduler won't pick it. The Code Predictor does its work, sends back a summed_embeddings, and only then does the engine flip Talker back to WAITING so it can take its next step. It's genuine ping-pong: step, pause, wait for the partner, resume. Expressing that cleanly is why the runtime needs an explicit notion of request state with pause and resume points — a plain streaming pipe couldn't capture it. Both patterns are invisible in a static DAG drawing. The DAG tells you the topology; these tell you the timing . And the timing is the actual product. Takeaways Coming back to where I started: SGLang-Omni taught me that for this class of model, the interesting engineering isn’t in the algorithms — it’s in the serving system . It’s decoupling, not a new algorithm. The core move is splitting one logical model into independent stages that run as separate processes. That’s what unlocks everything else. Right hardware, right scheduler, per stage. Two equal-sized decode backbones make placement and KV-cache/GPU-memory partitioning the central problem. Encoders and vocoders get lightweight one-shot executors; Thinker and Talker get full serving loops. One size does not fit all. Scale and trim by stage. Bottleneck at Thinker? Scale Thinker. No speech needed? Drop the whole speech chain via config. The pipeline bends to the workload. Separate the ticket from the plate. The control-plane / data-plane split — tiny ZMQ notifications alongside zero-copy tensor transport with credit-based backpressure — is what makes multi-process cheap instead of copy-heavy. Compose, don’t fork. The compute-heavy autoregressive stages delegate to SGLang and reuse RadixAttention, fused kernels, and its ModelRunner. Omni adds orchestration around SGLang; it doesn’t replace it. I came in expecting a bag of modality-specific speed tricks. What I found was a runtime whose entire job is coordination in time — getting a committee of models to see, think, and speak in a smooth, streamed, fault-tolerant flow. The model was never the hard part. The pipeline was. SGLang-Omni: The Model Was Never the Hard Part was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
How SGLang serves a model that sees, hears, and talks back — and why it needed a whole new runtime on top of SGLang.The misconception I started with

When I first heard about SGLang-Omni, I assumed I knew what it was.

SGLang, the core project, is famous for making a single large language model fast — RadixAttention for KV-cache reuse, speculative decoding, a zero-overhead scheduler, all the clever tricks that squeeze more tokens per second out of a GPU. So “Omni,” I figured, must be the same bag of tricks applied to other modalities. Some radix-cache-like reuse for audio. Some speculative decoding for image tokens. Modality-specific algorithmic wins.

That guess was wrong, and the way it was wrong turned out to be the interesting part.

SGLang-Omni is not a set of per-modality algorithm optimizations. It’s a systems-level orchestration play. Its whole reason to exist is to take a model that isn’t one model at all — it’s a little committee of models that talk to each other — and decouple it into independent stages, so you can:

  • put each stage on the right hardware,
  • give each stage the scheduler it actually needs,
  • scale up only the stage that’s the bottleneck,
  • and contain a crash to one stage instead of taking down the whole request.

In other words, the hard problem was never “make the model faster.” The model math was mostly already solved. The hard problem was serving it: how do you run a graph of cooperating models, streaming state between them in real time, across multiple GPUs, without the whole thing turning into a tangle?

This post walks through how SGLang-Omni answers that, using Qwen3-Omni as the running example. We’ll follow one request from HTTP call to audio waveform, and along the way see why a plain script couldn’t do the job, how the pipeline is wired, and — importantly — how Omni leans on plain old SGLang for the heavy lifting rather than reinventing it.

What Qwen3-Omni actually demands

To see why Omni needed a new runtime, you have to look at what a modern omni-modal model actually is. Core SGLang is built to serve one autoregressive model behind one scheduler and one KV cache. Qwen3-Omni is a committee.

Diagram 1 — The mental shift: one model vs a pipeline of stages.

Qwen3-Omni isn’t a single autoregressive model. It’s built around two large decode backbones that hand off to each other:

  • Thinker — the “understanding” brain. It takes text, images, video, and audio, fuses them, and generates text tokens. This is where the reasoning lives.
  • Talker — the “speaking” brain. It takes Thinker’s output as it’s being produced and turns it into a stream of speech codec tokens, which a vocoder later turns into an actual waveform.

Around those two, there’s a supporting cast: a vision encoder, an audio encoder, an aggregation step, a code predictor that fills in the fine detail of the audio codes, and a final vocoder. But the two things that dominate everything are Thinker and Talker.

Here’s what makes this genuinely different from serving one LLM:

  • Two backbones of roughly equal size. This is the crux. It’s not “one big model plus some small helpers.” Thinker and Talker are both heavy, both need continuous batching, both maintain a KV cache. The moment you have two comparably-sized models, you have a placement and resource-partitioning problem: do they share a GPU or not? If they share, how do you split GPU memory and KV cache between them — is 50/50 even right? If they don’t, how do you coordinate the traffic between devices? This is the real engineering pressure, far more than “supporting a vocoder.”
  • Dual output. A single request can produce two results — a text answer and an audio answer. The system can’t just return whichever finishes first; it has to gather both.
  • Real streaming between models. Talker doesn’t wait for Thinker to finish. It consumes Thinker’s hidden states token by token, so audio can start playing while the text is still being generated.
  • A feedback loop. Talker and the Code Predictor play ping-pong: Talker emits one codec token, waits for the Code Predictor to send back an aggregated embedding, and only then takes its next step.

None of these is a “just add a component” problem. They’re all about timing and coordination — who can run when, who’s waiting on whom, and where the intermediate state lives. That’s a scheduling and dataflow problem, and it’s exactly the kind of thing a single-model server isn’t built to express.

Why a serial script — or even asyncio — can’t do it

The natural first reaction is: if core SGLang doesn’t handle this, why not just write a function that chains the models together?

# The most naive serial approach
def process_request(request):
    state        = preprocess(request)                 # CPU
    image_embeds = image_encoder(state)                # GPU
    audio_embeds = audio_encoder(state)                # GPU — only starts after image_encoder finishes
    merged       = aggregate(state, image_embeds, audio_embeds)  # CPU
    text_tokens  = thinker(merged)                     # GPU:0 — next step only after thinker fully finishes
    text_result  = decode(text_tokens)                 # CPU
    codec_tokens = talker(text_tokens)                 # GPU:1 — only starts after thinker fully finishes
    codes        = code_predictor(codec_tokens)        # GPU:1
    audio        = code2wav(codes)                     # GPU:1
    return text_result, audio

This runs. It’s also a performance disaster, and the reason is subtle enough to be worth a number.

Talker has to wait until Thinker is completely done before it starts. Say Thinker generates 100 tokens at 30 ms each, and Talker takes 20 ms per step. Serial time-to-first-audio is roughly 3000 ms + 20 ms ≈ 3020 ms. But if Talker could consume Thinker’s tokens as they arrive, time-to-first-audio drops to about 30 ms + 20 ms ≈ 50 ms. That’s a ~60× difference in perceived latency, and it comes entirely from overlapping work that the serial version forces into a line.

So the next instinct is: fine, use asyncio, fire the encoders off in parallel, stream Thinker into Talker. That’s better — it at least admits the stages can advance concurrently. But single-process async only pushes the real problems back one layer. Five of them survive:

  1. GPU-memory isolation. Thinker is on GPU:0, Talker on GPU:1. Managing multiple large models across multiple GPUs in one process couples their CUDA contexts, memory allocation, and error handling. One model’s OOM becomes everyone’s problem. Separate processes give each stage its own clean device view.
  2. Different scheduling policies. Thinker needs continuous batching, KV-cache management, and dynamic batch changes. The Code Predictor is a lightweight step-by-step forward. Cramming both into one scheduler means either a monstrous unified abstraction or a pile of special-cased local logic. Split into stages, each stage picks the executor and policy that fits it.
  3. Fault isolation. In production, one model hanging or crashing shouldn’t kill the whole request chain. Process boundaries turn a stage crash into a stage crash.
  4. Bottleneck-only scaling. If Thinker is the bottleneck, you want to scale just Thinker. If a request doesn’t need speech, you want to drop Talker / Code Predictor / vocoder entirely. Stages make that a config change, not a rewrite.
  5. Control/data separation. Multi-process doesn’t have to mean “copy tensors everywhere.” The trick — which we’ll get to — is to send tiny metadata between stages (“the data is at this shared-memory slot”) while the big tensors move over shared memory or CUDA IPC, near zero-copy.

Put together, these push you toward a specific shape: a multi-process, asynchronous producer–consumer pipeline, where each stage is its own process, upstream stages produce incremental results, and downstream stages consume them at their own pace.

That shape is SGLang-Omni.

The answer: a pipeline of stages

At the top, SGLang-Omni is three layers:

Diagram 2 — The three-layer runtime.
  • The Coordinator is the front door and the mailroom. It does exactly three things: wrap the incoming request and hand it to the first stage; wait for the terminal stages to report back and merge their results; and, if the user disconnects, broadcast an “abort” to everyone. Crucially, it does not route between stages — it doesn’t decide “where does the encoder’s output go next.” Each stage decides that for itself via its own get_next. The Coordinator is a gatekeeper and a gatherer, not a traffic cop.
  • Stage → Worker → Executor is where a request actually gets computed. The Stage is a runtime shell: it receives messages, aggregates inputs when several upstream stages feed into it, and manages routing. The Worker is the execution unit inside a stage. The Executor is the thing that finally calls the model.
  • Control plane + Data plane is how stages communicate — and this split is the single most important idea in the whole system.
The waiter and the food runner

Here’s the intuition. In a restaurant, the waiter carries the order ticket — small, fast, “table 4 wants the salmon.” The food runner carries the plate — big, heavy, needs care. You don’t make the waiter carry plates, and you don’t make the runner memorize orders.

SGLang-Omni splits communication exactly this way:

  • Control plane (ZMQ): the order tickets. Tens of bytes, microsecond latency. “Stage A finished; the result for request 7 is sitting in shared-memory slot 2.” That’s it.
  • Data plane (the Relay): the plates. The actual tensors — encoder outputs, hidden states — move over shared memory, CUDA IPC, or NCCL, essentially zero-copy. They never touch ZMQ.
Diagram 3 — Control plane vs data plane, and the credit system.

The reason to separate them is that notifications and bulk data have opposite requirements. ZMQ is great for small control messages and terrible for moving giant tensors; shared memory and CUDA IPC are the reverse. Try to make one channel do both and you do neither well.

The Relay also needs flow control, and it uses a beautifully simple mechanism: credits, which is really just a semaphore. Picture a fixed number of serving trays between two kitchen stations — say two trays. A “credit” is an empty tray.

  • Upstream wants to send data → it takes a credit (grabs a tray), writes the tensor into that shared-memory slot, and sends a “data ready” ticket over ZMQ.
  • Downstream reads the data → releases the credit (returns the tray) so upstream can reuse the slot.
  • When all trays are full and downstream hasn’t caught up → upstream blocks. That’s backpressure, and it’s exactly what you want: a slow downstream naturally throttles a fast upstream instead of blowing up memory.

This is why downstream stages are built to read incoming data as fast as they can — every read frees a tray and keeps the line moving.

Add a model without touching the backbone

One design choice makes this framework more than a Qwen3-Omni special case: the pipeline topology isn’t hardcoded. It’s declarative config. A model doesn’t inherit a fixed set of steps — it declares its own stage graph, and the framework compiles that into a runnable pipeline.

# sglang_omni/models/qwen3_omni/config.py  (trimmed)
class Qwen3OmniSpeechPipelineConfig(PipelineConfig):
    entry_stage     = "preprocessing"
    terminal_stages = ["decode", "code2wav"]        # two ends: text + speech
    gpu_placement   = {"thinker": 0, "talker_ar": 1, "code_predictor": 1, "code2wav": 1}
    stages = [
        StageConfig("preprocessing", get_next=preprocessing_next, ...),
        StageConfig("image_encoder", get_next=encoder_next, ...),
        StageConfig("audio_encoder", get_next=encoder_next, ...),
        StageConfig("mm_aggregate",  get_next=aggregate_next,
                    input_handler=AggregatedInput(sources=["preprocessing",
                                                           "image_encoder",
                                                           "audio_encoder"])),
        StageConfig("thinker", get_next=thinker_next_speech,
                    stream_to=["talker_ar"]),               # stream hidden states
        StageConfig("decode", get_next=None),               # terminal
        StageConfig("talker_ar", get_next=talker_ar_next,
                    stream_to=["code_predictor"]),
        StageConfig("code_predictor", get_next=code_predictor_next,
                    stream_to=["code2wav", "talker_ar"]),   # dual path: output + feedback
        StageConfig("code2wav", get_next=None),             # terminal
    ]

Notice how much of the system’s behavior is data here: which stage is the entry, which are terminals, which GPU each stage lives on, which stages stream to which. compile_pipeline() turns this into live processes.

The payoff showed up when the team later added Ming-Omni, whose speech path uses a completely different approach (CFM/DiT flow-matching instead of Qwen3-Omni’s RVQ codec). The framework backbone barely changed — they wrote a new PipelineConfig and the model-specific executors, and the pipeline machinery just carried it. Model differences got pushed into config and executors, not into the runtime's core. There's even a variant mechanism so the same model can expose a 6-stage text-only pipeline and a 9-stage text-plus-speech pipeline, chosen at startup with --variant speech.

Walk one request through the nine stages

Let’s follow a “text + image + audio” request through Qwen3-Omni’s full speech pipeline. With speech output on, it’s nine stages:

STAGE            ROLE               DEVICE   WHAT IT DOES
─────────────    ────────────────   ──────   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
preprocessing    Entry              CPU      Tokenize text; parse image/audio/video into tensors
image_encoder    Encode             GPU      Vision Transformer → image embeddings
audio_encoder    Encode             GPU      Mel-spectrogram encoder → audio embeddings
aggregate        Fan-in             CPU      Merge text tokens with encoder outputs into one input
thinker          Inference          GPU:0    MoE Transformer; generates text tokens (then fans out)
decode           Output (terminal)  CPU      Turn token ids back into text
talker_ar        Speech             GPU:1    Autoregressively generate speech codec tokens
code_predictor   Speech             GPU:1    Fill in remaining RVQ code layers (feedback loop)
code2wav         Speech (terminal)  GPU:1    Vocoder synthesizes the final audio waveform
Diagram 4 — The Qwen3-Omni 9-stage pipeline. Note the fan-out (one input, many branches) at preprocessing and the fan-in (many branches, one input) at aggregate — plus the second fan-out at Thinker, where text and speech split.

Reading the flow:

  1. Preprocessing (CPU) turns raw input into tensors and metadata. The instant it’s done, the result fans out to three places at once — the image encoder, the audio encoder, and the aggregate stage. True parallelism starts here, not at the model.
  2. Image & audio encoders (GPU) run independently and in parallel. The image encoder is a Vision Transformer; the audio encoder is a Transformer over Mel-spectrogram features. Each sends its embeddings to aggregate.
  3. Aggregate (CPU) is the classic fan-in node. It waits until all its upstream inputs have arrived, then merges the text tokens with the encoder outputs into a single input Thinker can consume in one shot. It does little compute — its job is synchronization.
  4. Thinker (GPU:0) is the semantic center. It embeds the tokens, injects the encoder outputs at the right placeholder positions, runs its Transformer stack, and generates text tokens. Then it fans out again — the most important branch in the system, because this is where text and speech formally split:
    A. the text branch sends the full result to decode;
    B. the speech branch streams to talker_ar token by token, passing along not just the token ids but Thinker's embeddings and a chosen layer's hidden states, so Talker can align to what Thinker meant.
  5. Decode (CPU, terminal) turns Thinker’s token ids back into text and reports completion.
  6. Talker AR → Code Predictor → Code2Wav (GPU:1) is the speech chain. Talker autoregressively generates codec tokens; the Code Predictor fills in the fine-grained RVQ layers (and feeds information back to Talker, more on that below); Code2Wav — a neural vocoder — accumulates codes and streams out 24 kHz audio chunks.

When both terminals — decode and code2wav — report done, the Coordinator merges the text and the audio and returns them together.

How Omni rides on SGLang

Here’s the part I most misjudged at the start, and the part worth being precise about: SGLang-Omni is not a fork of SGLang. It’s an orchestration layer that sits on top of SGLang and treats it as a library for the compute-heavy work.

Think of it as a division of labor:

Diagram 5 — Omni owns the pipeline; SGLang owns the AR math

The heavy autoregressive stages — Thinker and Talker — are the ones that need everything core SGLang is good at: continuous batching, KV-cache management, fast attention. So Omni doesn’t rebuild any of that. Those stages run through an EngineExecutor wrapping OmniEngine, a compact serving loop with its own Scheduler (picks requests, builds batches) and ModelRunner (runs the forward). And that ModelRunner stands on SGLang's shoulders — the Thinker model, for example, reuses:

  • RadixAttention for efficient KV-cache management,
  • SGLang’s fused kernels (like a fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel for a big speedup),
  • and the same ModelRunner / forward / sampling machinery SGLang uses to serve a plain LLM.

The lighter stages don’t need any of this. An image encoder is a one-shot operator: input in, forward once, output out. It runs through a much thinner DirectModelExecutor — no request state, no KV cache, no scheduler. This is the whole point of the Executor abstraction:

class Executor(ABC):
    async def add_request(payload) -> None    # submit
    async def get_result() -> StagePayload     # collect
    async def abort(request_id) -> None        # cancel
    def set_stream_fn(fn) -> None              # streaming hook

Same interface, wildly different implementations — a stateless forward for encoders, a stateful multi-step engine for Thinker and Talker. The pipeline doesn’t care which; it just calls add_request and awaits get_result.

One more detail earns a single sentence: OmniEngine supports an overlap mode that runs the current step's GPU work while the CPU processes the previous step's results, the same GPU/CPU pipelining trick that made core SGLang's scheduler "zero-overhead." Omni reuses the idea rather than the exact code.

So the mental model is: Omni owns when and where things run; SGLang owns how the autoregressive math runs. Everything speech-specific — encoders, vocoders, streaming audio, the pipeline itself — is Omni’s. The transformer decode loop is SGLang’s.

The two clever tricks

Most of the pipeline is boring in a good way: stage finishes, next stage picks up. But two relationships aren’t like that, and they’re where “temporal orchestration” stops being a phrase and starts being code.

Diagram 6 — Streaming (Thinker→Talker) and the feedback loop (Talker↔Code Predictor).

① Streaming (stream_to). Thinker doesn't hand Talker a finished paragraph. Every time it generates a token, it immediately pushes the corresponding hidden states out. Talker consumes them as a true producer–consumer stream:

  • If Thinker is faster, a few tokens queue up and Talker catches up at its own pace.
  • If Talker is faster, the queue empties and Talker simply awaits the next token.
  • When Thinker finishes, it appends an end-of-text marker to the stream, and once Talker consumes it, Talker knows the text is done.

There’s even a nice optimization on startup: if Talker finds several tokens already waiting when it begins, it prefills on the whole batch at once instead of crawling forward one token at a time.

② The feedback loop (WAITING_FEEDBACK). This is the most intricate state transition in the system. Every time Talker emits a codec token, it can't just barrel ahead. It sends the token to the Code Predictor and deliberately parks itself in a WAITING_FEEDBACK state — and while it's parked, the scheduler won't pick it. The Code Predictor does its work, sends back a summed_embeddings, and only then does the engine flip Talker back to WAITING so it can take its next step. It's genuine ping-pong: step, pause, wait for the partner, resume. Expressing that cleanly is why the runtime needs an explicit notion of request state with pause and resume points — a plain streaming pipe couldn't capture it.

Both patterns are invisible in a static DAG drawing. The DAG tells you the topology; these tell you the timing. And the timing is the actual product.

Takeaways

Coming back to where I started: SGLang-Omni taught me that for this class of model, the interesting engineering isn’t in the algorithms — it’s in the serving system.

  • It’s decoupling, not a new algorithm. The core move is splitting one logical model into independent stages that run as separate processes. That’s what unlocks everything else.
  • Right hardware, right scheduler, per stage. Two equal-sized decode backbones make placement and KV-cache/GPU-memory partitioning the central problem. Encoders and vocoders get lightweight one-shot executors; Thinker and Talker get full serving loops. One size does not fit all.
  • Scale and trim by stage. Bottleneck at Thinker? Scale Thinker. No speech needed? Drop the whole speech chain via config. The pipeline bends to the workload.
  • Separate the ticket from the plate. The control-plane / data-plane split — tiny ZMQ notifications alongside zero-copy tensor transport with credit-based backpressure — is what makes multi-process cheap instead of copy-heavy.
  • Compose, don’t fork. The compute-heavy autoregressive stages delegate to SGLang and reuse RadixAttention, fused kernels, and its ModelRunner. Omni adds orchestration around SGLang; it doesn’t replace it.

I came in expecting a bag of modality-specific speed tricks. What I found was a runtime whose entire job is coordination in time — getting a committee of models to see, think, and speak in a smooth, streamed, fault-tolerant flow. The model was never the hard part. The pipeline was.

SGLang-Omni: The Model Was Never the Hard Part was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Agentic AI in Action — Part 28 — A Geospatial Store Intelligence Agent in Snowflake
items.summary: A Geospatial Store Intelligence Agent in Snowflake A look at how Semantic Views and Cortex Analyst answer store performance questions, while native geography functions draw the map. This blog walks through a store intelligence notebook, plain English questions answered through Cortex Analyst and Semantic Views, store locations plotted through native geography functions. The use case is straightforward. A retail chain wants store managers and regional planners to ask plain English questions about footfall and location, things like “show me stores in Chicago with footfall below 500 last month” , and get back both the matching rows and a rendered map. The pieces that make this possible, a Semantic View for Cortex Analyst, native geography functions for radius queries, and simple, popular Python packages like matplotlib for the visual layer, already exist inside Snowflake Notebooks. Nothing needs to be stitched together from outside services, and nothing fancy is required to render the output either. Along the way this also surfaces a useful design pattern. Cortex Analyst is genuinely good at turning language into SQL over the dimensions and metrics you have exposed to it, and pairing it with native SQL for spatial math gives each piece the job it is best suited for. That division, natural language for attribute filtering, native SQL for geometry, is what it actually comes down to. The architecture A single STORE_LOCATIONS table holds each store's id, city, footfall for the last month, and a GEOGRAPHY column built from latitude and longitude. A Semantic View sits on top of this table and exposes the dimensions and metrics Cortex Analyst needs to translate a natural language question into SQL. The distance filtering itself uses Snowflake's native ST_DWITHIN function against the geography column, so radius queries run as ordinary SQL rather than anything bolted on. The notebook is built around four US cities, New York, Chicago, Austin, and Seattle, with roughly eighty synthetic stores jittered around each city center so the points land in realistic locations without needing a real estate dataset. Generating the synthetic data Let’s begin by creating dedicated database and schema. We will generate roughly eighty stores spread across four US cities, New York, Chicago, Austin, and Seattle, each with a footfall reading for the last month. Coordinates are jittered around each city center so the points fall in relatively realistic locations without needing a real estate dataset. Each city gets twenty stores with footfall figures spread widely enough that a “below 500” style filter returns a meaningful subset rather than an empty result or the whole table. The Semantic View Semantic Views give Cortex Analyst a governed, business friendly layer over raw tables, defining dimensions, metrics, and join logic once so that natural language questions resolve consistently instead of relying on the model to guess at SQL each time. (For details on how semantic views work, please refer to Part 23 of my Agentic AI in Action series). In this cell, STORE_SEMANTIC_VIEW is created over the STORE_LOCATIONS table, keyed on store_id. It exposes city and store_name as dimensions, so questions can be sliced by location or by individual store, and defines two metrics, avg_footfall as the average of footfall_last_month and store_count as a count of store_id. When Cortex Analyst answers a question like which city has the highest average footfall, it resolves it against these definitions rather than improvising the aggregation, and the same city and footfall groupings carry through cleanly into the pydeck map later in the notebook. This is deliberately narrow. Cortex Analyst only needs enough structure to translate “stores in Chicago with low footfall” into a WHERE clause and an aggregation. Notice what’s missing, latitude, longitude, and anything geography-flavored aren’t in here at all. That’s on purpose, and it matters for what comes next. Splitting the work between Cortex Analyst and native SQL Cortex Analyst is scoped to whatever the Semantic View exposes, city and footfall in this case, so questions about attributes and aggregates go to it directly. Distance is a different kind of question, geometry rather than filtering, and Snowflake already has native functions for that. The cleaner pattern keeps the two separate. Cortex Analyst handles “which stores, filtered by which attributes,” and a direct query against the GEOGRAPHY column built in Cell 2 handles “which stores, within this radius.” This runs on its own using Snowflake’s native ST_DWITHIN function whenever the question genuinely needs distance math, radius searches, nearest neighbor lookups, and so on. Cortex Analyst picks up from there for the attribute filtering that follows. Running this against the actual data returns all 20 Chicago stores, footfall ranging from 233 up to 1,379. With the jitter radius used to scatter stores around each city center, a 25 km search from downtown Chicago comfortably covers every store tagged to that city, which is a useful sanity check in itself, the geometry is doing exactly what it should. Asking the question This cell creates a reusable Python function called ask_cortex_analyst() to send a natural-language question to Snowflake Cortex Analyst. The function takes the user’s question and, by default, the semantic view GEO_DEMO.RETAIL.STORE_SEMANTIC_VIEW, which we just created. It then obtains the Snowflake connection, authentication token, and account host from the existing Snowpark session and constructs the Cortex Analyst REST API endpoint. The question and semantic view are packaged into a JSON payload and sent to the API using an HTTP POST request, with the Snowflake token included for authentication. The function waits up to 60 seconds for a response and checks the HTTP status code to determine whether the request was successful. If an error occurs, it prints the status and part of the error response and raises an exception; otherwise, it converts the API response from JSON into a Python object and returns it. In short, the cell acts as the bridge between a Python notebook and Cortex Analyst, allowing a user to ask business questions in natural language and receive Cortex Analyst’s response programmatically. At the bottom of the cell is the question: The question is scoped to city and footfall, since radius search belongs to the native SQL step above rather than to Cortex Analyst. That’s why the phrasing is “stores in Chicago” instead of “stores within 25 km,” and Cortex Analyst returns a clean SQL statement matching exactly that scope. In other words, this demonstrates how you can use Cortex Analyst not just to answer a business question, but to retrieve and inspect the SQL that it generated to answer that question. That’s the actual SQL Cortex Analyst generated for the question, wrapped in a CTE, filtered on CITY and FOOTFALL_LAST_MONTH, and ordered descending. There are no coordinates or distance calculations involved. It stays exactly within the scope supported by the Semantic View. Running it returns five stores as seen above. Rendering the map by latitude and longitude One more design detail before the map renders. The Semantic View scopes Cortex Analyst’s output to STORE_ID, STORE_NAME, CITY, and FOOTFALL_LAST_MONTH, the dimensions and metrics defined for it, so coordinates come back in through a join against STORE_LOCATIONS. This is a reasonable pattern in general, the app layer around Cortex Analyst enriches its output with anything outside the semantic model rather than assuming the result already carries everything a downstream step needs. Five Chicago stores under 500 footfall, plotted by latitude and longitude Store 24 sits well north of the other four, at the edge of the jittered coordinate spread, while the rest cluster closer to the city center. This is the payoff. The same question that started as a plain English sentence ends up as pins on a map, and the whole round trip, natural language in, SQL generated, query executed, coordinates joined back in, result rendered, happens inside one Notebook session using only pandas and matplotlib, both of which ship with every Snowflake Notebook by default. If your environment has streamlit and pydeck available through the Packages selector, the same map_df drops into a pdk.Layer and st.pydeck_chart for a more polished interactive map, but the matplotlib version is the one guaranteed to run without any package configuration. An optional layer for territory footfall Individual pins work well for a specific question, but a regional planner usually wants a rollup by territory rather than a list of points. Bucketing stores into H3 cells and summarizing average footfall per cell gives that view. H3 cells are Uber’s hexagonal grid system for dividing the map into uniform regions, and H3_POINT_TO_CELL_STRING(location, resolution) is Snowflake’s native function for looking up which hexagon a given point falls into, returning that hexagon’s ID as a string so stores in the same region can be grouped together with GROUP BY. That string is just an identifier, not a shape, so it’s enough to group and aggregate footfall by territory, but drawing the actual hexagon boundaries on a map needs geometry that pydeck’s H3HexagonLayer normally supplies. (Since this notebook stays dependency-light, the output here is a table and bar chart of cell IDs and their average footfall rather than rendered hexagons). We will go ahead and plot a bar chart summary of footfall by H3 territory. Top ten H3 territories by average footfall, one bar per H3 cell Each of these top cells holds exactly one store, which tracks with H3 resolution 7 at this scale, eighty stores spread across four metro areas, most stores land in their own cell. A coarser resolution, say H3_POINT_TO_CELL_STRING(LOCATION, 5), groups more stores per cell for a broader density read. This step turns “find nearby stores” into “identify underserved territories,” which tends to land better with a business audience than a list of individual points. (If pydeck is available in your environment, the same h3_df drops into an H3HexagonLayer for an actual hexagon map instead of a bar chart). What matters here isn’t the map, it’s where each piece of the work actually happens. Cortex Analyst handles the part it’s built for, turning a plain English question into SQL over a defined set of dimensions and metrics, and native SQL and Python handle the rest, geometry, joins, and rendering. There is no external service in the loop and no data leaves the account. Swap the underlying table and Semantic View metrics, warehouse footfall for logistics, branch traffic for banking, and the same pattern carries over with the Cortex Analyst and rendering cells unchanged. The notebook for this blog can be accessed here. I share hands-on, implementation-focused perspectives on Generative & Agentic AI, LLMs, Snowflake and Cortex AI, translating advanced capabilities into practical, real-world analytics use cases. Do follow me on LinkedIn and Medium for more such insights. items.summary_html:
A Geospatial Store Intelligence Agent in SnowflakeA look at how Semantic Views and Cortex Analyst answer store performance questions, while native geography functions draw the map.

This blog walks through a store intelligence notebook, plain English questions answered through Cortex Analyst and Semantic Views, store locations plotted through native geography functions.

The use case is straightforward. A retail chain wants store managers and regional planners to ask plain English questions about footfall and location, things like “show me stores in Chicago with footfall below 500 last month”, and get back both the matching rows and a rendered map. The pieces that make this possible, a Semantic View for Cortex Analyst, native geography functions for radius queries, and simple, popular Python packages like matplotlib for the visual layer, already exist inside Snowflake Notebooks. Nothing needs to be stitched together from outside services, and nothing fancy is required to render the output either.

Along the way this also surfaces a useful design pattern. Cortex Analyst is genuinely good at turning language into SQL over the dimensions and metrics you have exposed to it, and pairing it with native SQL for spatial math gives each piece the job it is best suited for. That division, natural language for attribute filtering, native SQL for geometry, is what it actually comes down to.

The architecture

A single STORE_LOCATIONS table holds each store's id, city, footfall for the last month, and a GEOGRAPHY column built from latitude and longitude. A Semantic View sits on top of this table and exposes the dimensions and metrics Cortex Analyst needs to translate a natural language question into SQL. The distance filtering itself uses Snowflake's native ST_DWITHIN function against the geography column, so radius queries run as ordinary SQL rather than anything bolted on.

The notebook is built around four US cities, New York, Chicago, Austin, and Seattle, with roughly eighty synthetic stores jittered around each city center so the points land in realistic locations without needing a real estate dataset.

Generating the synthetic data

Let’s begin by creating dedicated database and schema.

We will generate roughly eighty stores spread across four US cities, New York, Chicago, Austin, and Seattle, each with a footfall reading for the last month. Coordinates are jittered around each city center so the points fall in relatively realistic locations without needing a real estate dataset.

Each city gets twenty stores with footfall figures spread widely enough that a “below 500” style filter returns a meaningful subset rather than an empty result or the whole table.

The Semantic View

Semantic Views give Cortex Analyst a governed, business friendly layer over raw tables, defining dimensions, metrics, and join logic once so that natural language questions resolve consistently instead of relying on the model to guess at SQL each time.

(For details on how semantic views work, please refer to Part 23 of my Agentic AI in Action series).

In this cell, STORE_SEMANTIC_VIEW is created over the STORE_LOCATIONS table, keyed on store_id. It exposes city and store_name as dimensions, so questions can be sliced by location or by individual store, and defines two metrics, avg_footfall as the average of footfall_last_month and store_count as a count of store_id. When Cortex Analyst answers a question like which city has the highest average footfall, it resolves it against these definitions rather than improvising the aggregation, and the same city and footfall groupings carry through cleanly into the pydeck map later in the notebook.

This is deliberately narrow. Cortex Analyst only needs enough structure to translate “stores in Chicago with low footfall” into a WHERE clause and an aggregation. Notice what’s missing, latitude, longitude, and anything geography-flavored aren’t in here at all. That’s on purpose, and it matters for what comes next.

Splitting the work between Cortex Analyst and native SQL

Cortex Analyst is scoped to whatever the Semantic View exposes, city and footfall in this case, so questions about attributes and aggregates go to it directly. Distance is a different kind of question, geometry rather than filtering, and Snowflake already has native functions for that. The cleaner pattern keeps the two separate. Cortex Analyst handles “which stores, filtered by which attributes,” and a direct query against the GEOGRAPHY column built in Cell 2 handles “which stores, within this radius.”

This runs on its own using Snowflake’s native ST_DWITHIN function whenever the question genuinely needs distance math, radius searches, nearest neighbor lookups, and so on. Cortex Analyst picks up from there for the attribute filtering that follows.

Running this against the actual data returns all 20 Chicago stores, footfall ranging from 233 up to 1,379. With the jitter radius used to scatter stores around each city center, a 25 km search from downtown Chicago comfortably covers every store tagged to that city, which is a useful sanity check in itself, the geometry is doing exactly what it should.

Asking the question

This cell creates a reusable Python function called ask_cortex_analyst() to send a natural-language question to Snowflake Cortex Analyst. The function takes the user’s question and, by default, the semantic view GEO_DEMO.RETAIL.STORE_SEMANTIC_VIEW, which we just created. It then obtains the Snowflake connection, authentication token, and account host from the existing Snowpark session and constructs the Cortex Analyst REST API endpoint. The question and semantic view are packaged into a JSON payload and sent to the API using an HTTP POST request, with the Snowflake token included for authentication. The function waits up to 60 seconds for a response and checks the HTTP status code to determine whether the request was successful. If an error occurs, it prints the status and part of the error response and raises an exception; otherwise, it converts the API response from JSON into a Python object and returns it. In short, the cell acts as the bridge between a Python notebook and Cortex Analyst, allowing a user to ask business questions in natural language and receive Cortex Analyst’s response programmatically.

At the bottom of the cell is the question:

The question is scoped to city and footfall, since radius search belongs to the native SQL step above rather than to Cortex Analyst. That’s why the phrasing is “stores in Chicago” instead of “stores within 25 km,” and Cortex Analyst returns a clean SQL statement matching exactly that scope. In other words, this demonstrates how you can use Cortex Analyst not just to answer a business question, but to retrieve and inspect the SQL that it generated to answer that question.

That’s the actual SQL Cortex Analyst generated for the question, wrapped in a CTE, filtered on CITY and FOOTFALL_LAST_MONTH, and ordered descending. There are no coordinates or distance calculations involved. It stays exactly within the scope supported by the Semantic View.

Running it returns five stores as seen above.

Rendering the map by latitude and longitude

One more design detail before the map renders. The Semantic View scopes Cortex Analyst’s output to STORE_ID, STORE_NAME, CITY, and FOOTFALL_LAST_MONTH, the dimensions and metrics defined for it, so coordinates come back in through a join against STORE_LOCATIONS. This is a reasonable pattern in general, the app layer around Cortex Analyst enriches its output with anything outside the semantic model rather than assuming the result already carries everything a downstream step needs.

Five Chicago stores under 500 footfall, plotted by latitude and longitude

Store 24 sits well north of the other four, at the edge of the jittered coordinate spread, while the rest cluster closer to the city center. This is the payoff. The same question that started as a plain English sentence ends up as pins on a map, and the whole round trip, natural language in, SQL generated, query executed, coordinates joined back in, result rendered, happens inside one Notebook session using only pandas and matplotlib, both of which ship with every Snowflake Notebook by default. If your environment has streamlit and pydeck available through the Packages selector, the same map_df drops into a pdk.Layer and st.pydeck_chart for a more polished interactive map, but the matplotlib version is the one guaranteed to run without any package configuration.

An optional layer for territory footfall

Individual pins work well for a specific question, but a regional planner usually wants a rollup by territory rather than a list of points. Bucketing stores into H3 cells and summarizing average footfall per cell gives that view.

H3 cells are Uber’s hexagonal grid system for dividing the map into uniform regions, and H3_POINT_TO_CELL_STRING(location, resolution) is Snowflake’s native function for looking up which hexagon a given point falls into, returning that hexagon’s ID as a string so stores in the same region can be grouped together with GROUP BY. That string is just an identifier, not a shape, so it’s enough to group and aggregate footfall by territory, but drawing the actual hexagon boundaries on a map needs geometry that pydeck’s H3HexagonLayer normally supplies. (Since this notebook stays dependency-light, the output here is a table and bar chart of cell IDs and their average footfall rather than rendered hexagons).

We will go ahead and plot a bar chart summary of footfall by H3 territory.

Top ten H3 territories by average footfall, one bar per H3 cell

Each of these top cells holds exactly one store, which tracks with H3 resolution 7 at this scale, eighty stores spread across four metro areas, most stores land in their own cell. A coarser resolution, say H3_POINT_TO_CELL_STRING(LOCATION, 5), groups more stores per cell for a broader density read. This step turns “find nearby stores” into “identify underserved territories,” which tends to land better with a business audience than a list of individual points. (If pydeck is available in your environment, the same h3_df drops into an H3HexagonLayer for an actual hexagon map instead of a bar chart).

What matters here isn’t the map, it’s where each piece of the work actually happens.

Cortex Analyst handles the part it’s built for, turning a plain English question into SQL over a defined set of dimensions and metrics, and native SQL and Python handle the rest, geometry, joins, and rendering. There is no external service in the loop and no data leaves the account. Swap the underlying table and Semantic View metrics, warehouse footfall for logistics, branch traffic for banking, and the same pattern carries over with the Cortex Analyst and rendering cells unchanged.

The notebook for this blog can be accessed here.

items.title: One Canadian province is betting that being nice to Trump works
items.summary: Canada has stepped up efforts to promote domestically produced goods as its trade fight with the US has intensified. Graham Hughes/NurPhoto/Getty Images Alberta is betting on diplomacy with Trump while other Canadian provinces hit back. The province's top US envoy says the softer approach is winning Alberta better access in Washington. The bet is being tested as Canada and the US unleash a fresh round of tariffs. As Canada escalates its trade war with President Donald Trump, Alberta is betting on a softer approach. The oil-rich province has resisted some of the retaliation embraced elsewhere in Canada, while Premier Danielle Smith has pushed for more engagement with Washington. Alberta's top representative in the US says that strategy is getting results. "I think the premier's diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province," Nathan Cooper told CBC's "West of Centre" podcast published on Friday. "If we look at the impact of US tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact," Cooper said. Cooper said US officials have been "significantly more responsive" to Alberta than to some other provinces. Alberta is the only remaining province with neither a ban nor a retaliatory levy on US alcohol imports, a stance Cooper said American officials have shown "a real appreciation" for. "I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta as well," Cooper said. Alberta also has some insulation from the trade war. Energy is exempt from Trump's latest 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, while Canada remains by far the biggest source of US crude imports. Smith has rejected calls to use Alberta's oil as leverage against Washington, including proposals to tax or restrict exports. Meanwhile, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe has also argued that oil and potash should stay out of the fight, even as his province put a 50% levy on American alcohol into effect on Tuesday. The softer stance comes as the broader US-Canada trade fight escalates. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has struggled to reach a trade deal with Trump after months of negotiations. Canada's latest counter-tariffs take effect Tuesday, including 25% on US cheese and 50% on honey and aluminum foil. The retaliatory tariffs are in response to levies imposed by Trump last month on about $20 billion of Canadian goods after months of unsuccessful trade negotiations. items.summary_html:
Canada has stepped up efforts to promote domestically produced goods as its trade fight with the US has intensified.

Graham Hughes/NurPhoto/Getty Images

  • Alberta is betting on diplomacy with Trump while other Canadian provinces hit back.
  • The province's top US envoy says the softer approach is winning Alberta better access in Washington.
  • The bet is being tested as Canada and the US unleash a fresh round of tariffs.

As Canada escalates its trade war with President Donald Trump, Alberta is betting on a softer approach.

The oil-rich province has resisted some of the retaliation embraced elsewhere in Canada, while Premier Danielle Smith has pushed for more engagement with Washington.

Alberta's top representative in the US says that strategy is getting results.

"I think the premier's diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province," Nathan Cooper told CBC's "West of Centre" podcast published on Friday.

"If we look at the impact of US tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact," Cooper said.

Cooper said US officials have been "significantly more responsive" to Alberta than to some other provinces.

Alberta is the only remaining province with neither a ban nor a retaliatory levy on US alcohol imports, a stance Cooper said American officials have shown "a real appreciation" for.

"I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta as well," Cooper said.

Alberta also has some insulation from the trade war. Energy is exempt from Trump's latest 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, while Canada remains by far the biggest source of US crude imports.

Smith has rejected calls to use Alberta's oil as leverage against Washington, including proposals to tax or restrict exports.

Meanwhile, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe has also argued that oil and potash should stay out of the fight, even as his province put a 50% levy on American alcohol into effect on Tuesday.

The softer stance comes as the broader US-Canada trade fight escalates.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has struggled to reach a trade deal with Trump after months of negotiations.

Canada's latest counter-tariffs take effect Tuesday, including 25% on US cheese and 50% on honey and aluminum foil. The retaliatory tariffs are in response to levies imposed by Trump last month on about $20 billion of Canadian goods after months of unsuccessful trade negotiations.

The tensions have also spilled beyond trade.

Trump issued an executive order last month directing the US government to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America."

Apple Maps and Google Maps subsequently adopted the name for US users, while Canada continues to recognize it as Lake Ontario.
